familySensitivity.changedAxis: current check-in state for a strength-priority athlete with no wearable data
familySensitivity.rationale: The family differentiates correctly in direction: normal readiness trains fully, occupational fatigue reduces and delays load, and an active flare avoids every guardrail-restricted template without exception -- a real, verifiable safety fix. But the flare case overcorrects on the goal-fit axis: with no symptom-compatible substitute available in the template catalog for this scenario, the guardrail response degrades to a full two-week strength blackout rather than a tightened-but-present strength presence, and nothing in the case format lets a later day's settled check-in reopen strength work within the window. Across all three cases, off-goal generic filler (field/sprint technique in the fatigue case, walking/field in the flare case) repeatedly displaces the stated bench/deadlift specificity, which looks like the same underlying ranking gap surfacing at different severities.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery/time state and subjective-vs-wearable disagreement for a health-and-fat-loss evergreen athlete with Garmin data
familySensitivity.rationale: Recovery-signal handling is solid across the family -- adverse recovery and adverse-wearable-despite-good-subjective both produce appropriately conservative plans. The recurring, more serious problem is unrelated to recovery sensitivity: both the baseline and low-time cases insert a Hard Endurance running session for a persona whose preferred modalities are Strength/Walking/Cycling, who has no event, and whose entire goal framing is 'no reason to peak'. This is the same class of finding the original persona-judge baseline recorded for this exact family (tempo/hard running late in the two-week horizon) -- it does not appear to have been addressed by the shoulder/back safety fix this re-judge was primarily checking, and is worth tracking as its own separate follow-up.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery state for a former high-level endurance athlete whose present training is intermittent
familySensitivity.rationale: The family correctly avoids the two most obvious historical-fitness traps: low motivation alone doesn't trigger restriction, and adverse recovery isn't overridden by the athlete's elite background. The recurring soft spot is that both the baseline and low-motivation cases open with the single longest, highest-load strength template on their very first day despite zero current history -- not clearly wrong given the good same-day readiness, but also not obviously the conservative choice a 'sparse current history is the dose authority' persona calls for.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery, today-specific modality preference, and already-trained state for an evergreen balanced-performance generalist
familySensitivity.rationale: Adverse recovery and already-trained-today both produce clearly proportionate, directionally correct responses. The strength-preference case is the outlier: it produces the exact same plan as the unset-preference baseline, so this comparison pair doesn't demonstrate that preferredModalityToday actually influences selection -- it may simply be redundant with what the optimizer would already choose on a good-readiness day.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery/time state with a standing running restriction, heavy-lower-body guardrail, and no training equipment
familySensitivity.rationale: This is the most consistently solid family reviewed: three simultaneous hard constraints (modality restriction, loading guardrail, zero equipment) are respected in every case without exception, and recovery/time adaptations layer on top correctly rather than being traded off against the constraints. No infeasible slot ever needed reporting because walking and bodyweight strength remain genuinely available, so the 'report infeasibility' half of the comparison instruction isn't exercised here, but nothing in the output suggests it would fail to.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery/time state for a health-priority athlete who cannot run and prefers walking
familySensitivity.rationale: This family gets the core premise right throughout: walking is never treated as filler and is never silently replaced by the restricted Running modality, even under adverse recovery or a tight time cap. Recovery and time adaptations scale dose appropriately without abandoning the athlete's only viable aerobic modality.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: current recovery, motivation, and recent hard-session density for an endurance athlete with a genuinely established current training base
familySensitivity.rationale: This family's strongest result is what it correctly does NOT do: low motivation alone, with every other signal normal, produces no change from the good-recovery baseline, which is the right call per the stated methodology. Adverse recovery is handled proportionately. The recent-hard-load case shows correct same-day restraint but leaves the later-week hard-session placement not fully verifiable from a single input snapshot -- a genuine limit of this case format rather than a confirmed defect.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: recovery, local mechanical constraint, today-specific modality preference, and time availability for a cycling-primary hybrid athlete
familySensitivity.rationale: The family's safety-facing sensitivity is genuinely strong: adverse recovery and the good-wearable/active-guardrail conflict both produce exactly the proportionate, non-overridden responses the calibration asks for, and no guardrail-tagged template ever leaks through even when wearable data looks excellent. But the specificity-facing sensitivity is weak in two ways: the same-day strength preference has no visible effect versus baseline (also seen in the balanced-performance family, so likely a real engine behavior rather than persona-specific noise), and a tight time window drives the plan to near-total reliance on walking despite indoor-bike access, which contradicts this persona's entire premise as a cycling-primary athlete.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: A/B/C event priority for the same established runner, same scheduled 10K, same race date, same recovery and same current training history
familySensitivity.rationale: The A-priority case shows genuinely strong, correct taper restraint. But the B-to-C comparison inverts the expected gradient: C, the lowest-priority event, ends up with more total race-specific volume (two race-pace sessions, one as long as 90 minutes) than B, which uses a shorter race-pace session plus a taper-sharpen. This is a concrete, well-evidenced directional problem, not a marginal calibration nuance -- it's the opposite of what 'C should not be treated like a major peak by default' asks for.

familySensitivity.changedAxis: recovery, weekday capacity, and race proximity for one established Olympic-distance triathlete
familySensitivity.rationale: This is the strongest family reviewed. Build-phase and taper-phase cases are both clearly differentiated in the correct direction, recovery signals scale dose without dropping a discipline, and taper execution specifically (short openers, technique work, minimal strength) matches what the final 14 days before an A-event should look like. This is consistent with the recently-landed Olympic-triathlon taper/recovery-reentry/weekday-cap fix.

caseScores.rationale: Normal readiness with no pain produces two free-weight full-body sessions (bench/deadlift/press/row via str_full_01), a bodyweight full-body session, and a pull-up session across two weeks, with no wearable data invented anywhere. The stated bench/deadlift emphasis is present but only in 2 of 5 strength exposures; the rest is generic bodyweight/pull-up work plus three walks, which is a real but modest specificity gap.
suggestedChanges: Bias the weekly strength slots toward the free-weight full-body template over the bodyweight/pull-up variants when the persona's stated goal is bench/deadlift-specific and no guardrail restricts loaded work.
Use walking as a low-cost filler rather than displacing a strength slot when time/equipment allow another loaded session.

caseScores.rationale: High fatigue/soreness from a physically demanding job appropriately triggers an opening rest day and a reduced-dose session (str_full_03) before returning to a full free-weight session later in the window -- a sensible use of occupational load without a wearable. However, the plan twice inserts 'Sprint Mechanics Foundation' (Field/sprint-technique work), which has no connection to a stated maximal-strength, bench/deadlift goal and isn't in the athlete's preferred modalities; this reads as generic slot-filling once the weekly strength quota is met, at the expense of goal specificity.
suggestedChanges: Do not fill remaining weekly slots with an unrelated modality (field/sprint technique) for a persona whose stated goal and preferences are strength-only; prefer walking/mobility or another light strength exposure instead.
Once early fatigue eases, prefer restoring bench/deadlift-specific volume before other strength variants.

caseScores.rationale: Two opening rest days and the complete absence of any overhead-pressing or heavy-spinal-loading template correctly respect the active shoulder/back guardrails -- no unsafe session is ever selected. But the plan contains zero Strength-modality sessions across the entire 14-day horizon, filling every training day with Field maintenance or walking instead. The persona's stated goal explicitly asks to 'progress maximal strength without repeatedly aggravating shoulder or back symptoms', not to stop strength training entirely; no symptom-compatible strength substitute (e.g. lower-body-only or guardrail-exempt upper work) is ever offered, and nothing in the plan signals a re-check or a path back to strength work.
suggestedChanges: After the initial acute rest window, offer a symptom-compatible strength substitute (e.g. lower-body-focused or single-joint upper work that avoids overhead pressing and heavy spinal loading) rather than dropping the modality entirely for two weeks.

Surface a short rationale note explaining that shoulder/back guardrails are limiting today's options, so the absence of strength work reads as a deliberate safety response rather than an unexplained gap.
Gate re-entry to fuller strength programming on an explicit follow-up check-in rather than holding a flat restriction with no visible re-check.

caseScores.rationale: Normal recovery produces a mostly sensible walking/strength/mobility week, but day 12 inserts a full Hard Endurance Running session (30-60 min) even though Running isn't in this persona's preferred modalities (Strength, Walking, Cycling) and the persona explicitly has no event or reason to peak. This reads as invented performance-style intensity for a sustainable health/fat-loss goal.
suggestedChanges: Do not select a Hard-tier session in a non-preferred modality for an event-free health persona; if higher intensity is warranted, use it within a preferred modality (e.g. a harder cycling or strength dose) at a Moderate rather than Hard tier.

caseScores.rationale: Two rest days plus mobility, then a graded walking re-entry before a single free-weight strength session near the end, is a proportionate response to a 14-point HRV drop and poor sleep, without inventing calorie targets or crash-diet framing.

The 30-minute cap is respected mechanically throughout (reduced-dose strength, capped walking), which is good. But the same Hard Endurance running session reappears on day 12, now fit into the 30-minute window (25-30 min) rather than dropped -- the same non-preferred-modality, unnecessary-intensity issue as the baseline case, just resized rather than reconsidered.
suggestedChanges: Same as baseline: this persona's stated modality preferences and no-peak goal should exclude a Hard Endurance running session regardless of time-window fit.

caseScores.rationale: Despite excellent subjective readiness (8/10, high motivation, low fatigue), a 14-point HRV drop and a body-battery reading of 24 correctly produce a conservative plan rather than letting the good self-report override clearly adverse objective data. The resulting plan is byte-identical to the concordant-adverse-recovery case, though, so this comparison doesn't demonstrate the system actually reasons about a subjective/objective conflict differently from agreement -- the conservative direction is defensible, but the lack of any visible distinction between 'both sources agree it's bad' and 'sources disagree, objective wins' is worth noting.
suggestedChanges: If subjective/objective conflict is meant to be judged differently from concordant adverse signals (e.g. a smaller, not identical, reduction), verify that distinction actually exists in the ranking logic rather than collapsing to the same output.

caseScores.rationale: With zero logged current history but excellent day-zero readiness, the week is mostly conservative (reduced/easy running, a bodyweight strength session, two rest days, mobility), and the two moderate running sessions only appear late in week two -- broadly consistent with 'rebuild from current response, not historical fitness'. The one point worth watching: day one opens with the longest, highest-load strength template (str_full_01, 45-60 min) rather than a shorter introductory session, which is harder to justify purely from a single good-readiness day with no current training history behind it.
suggestedChanges: Consider defaulting a genuinely sparse-history athlete's first strength exposure to a shorter/reduced-dose template even on a good-readiness day, reserving the full-dose template for after at least one completed session establishes current tolerance.

caseScores.rationale: Two rest days plus mobility and a graded easy-running re-entry proportionately respect the adverse HRV/sleep drop. A full-dose str_full_01 session appears on day six, which is plausible if the intervening days allowed genuine recovery, but a single-day input snapshot can't confirm the forecast actually re-derives current tolerance rather than assuming a return to baseline capacity.

With fatigue/soreness/objective signals all normal and only motivation low, the plan matches the good-readiness baseline rather than either inflating load from the athlete's elite history or needlessly restricting it from low motivation alone -- both correct per this family's calibration.

Good readiness and healthy Garmin baselines produce a genuinely mixed week: three strength sessions (full-weight, bodyweight, reduced), five running sessions building from easy to tempo, one walk, mobility, and two rest days, with no invented event or taper drama for this event-free generalist.
suggestedChanges: Nothing significant; consider spacing the two tempo runs (days 11 and 13) a day further apart from each other for cleaner quality-session separation.

caseScores.rationale: Two opening rest days plus mobility, then a graded re-entry through light running and walking before strength resumes, is a proportionate response to a 14-point HRV drop and a poor-sleep night -- neither ignoring the signal nor overreacting into a full-week shutdown.

The resulting 14-day plan is byte-identical to the baseline case, even though this case sets preferredModalityToday to 'Strength' while baseline leaves it unset. The plan itself is reasonable (day one was already a strength session in both cases), but the preference's effect on selection is not observable from this input pair -- it's unclear whether the signal is being honored or is simply moot here.
suggestedChanges: Construct a comparison case where the optimizer's default choice and the today-preference disagree, so the preference's actual effect on selection can be verified rather than assumed.

caseScores.rationale: Despite excellent readiness, 'already trained today' correctly produces Rest for today only -- no duplicate substantive session is added -- while strength and running both resume normally from day two onward. This is exactly the same-day-execution-fact handling the comparison instruction calls for, not a slide into chronic recovery.

With Running restricted, avoid_heavy_lower_body active, and zero training equipment, the plan uses only bodyweight full-body strength and walking -- both genuinely compatible -- with no attempt to work around the restriction or equipment gap. Cycling stays unreached despite being preferred, which is a real (not fabricated) equipment infeasibility, not an engine bug.

Two rest days plus mobility, then a graded walking re-entry with one bodyweight strength session, respects both the adverse recovery signal and the standing injury/equipment constraints simultaneously without either one being dropped to satisfy the other.

The 30-minute cap is respected (day-one strength reduced to 15-25 min) while the injury/equipment restrictions remain intact throughout -- three simultaneous hard constraints handled without any of them being silently relaxed.

Walking appears repeatedly as substantial, full-dose training (up to the 60-minute ceiling), not token filler, alongside three genuine strength sessions -- and Running never appears anywhere in the plan despite being a common default endurance template elsewhere in the catalog.

Two rest days plus mobility, then reduced-duration walking rather than dropping the modality entirely, is a proportionate response to the HRV/sleep drop that still keeps the athlete's only available aerobic modality meaningfully present.

Under the 30-minute cap, walking sessions are capped exactly at 30 minutes and strength is reduced to 15-25 minutes rather than either being dropped -- the plan still delivers real aerobic and strength volume within the constraint rather than defaulting to rest.

Good readiness produces a sensible easy-volume week with two moderate-intensity sessions layered on top -- genuine 'purposeful quality on top of established aerobic volume' as the goal states, with no invented event or taper drama for this event-free persona.
Two opening rest days plus mobility, then a graded easy-volume re-entry, is proportionate to a 14-point HRV drop and poor sleep, without discarding the runner's established base.

With fatigue, soreness and every objective signal reading normal and only motivation reported low, the plan is identical to the good-recovery baseline -- correctly not treating low motivation alone as a physiological red flag, exactly as the judge methodology specifies.

Today correctly downgrades to a capped, modify-mode easy run despite good readiness, respecting the two hard sessions in the prior three days rather than stacking a third. A full Hard Endurance session then appears six days later (day 7), which is plausible if the intervening moderate session and rest day allowed real recovery, but a single-day snapshot doesn't let me verify that the recent-hard-session context actually decays correctly across the forecast rather than a later day simply not seeing it at all.
suggestedChanges: Confirm (via a dedicated test, not just this persona snapshot) that last_3_days_hard_sessions_count-style context decays realistically across a multi-day forecast rather than only applying to day zero.

caseScores.rationale: Good readiness produces only 3 cycling sessions against 4 walking sessions and one moderate running session (day 13), even though this athlete self-describes as cycling-primary and Running is explicitly deprioritized. Strength retention (3 sessions) is well represented. For a self-described cycling-primary athlete, walking outnumbering cycling is a real specificity gap, not a safety concern.
suggestedChanges: Prefer an additional cycling session over walking once strength's weekly role is satisfied, given cycling is the stated primary performance objective.
Avoid selecting a deprioritized modality (Running) when the primary modality (Cycling) remains available and time/equipment allow it.

caseScores.rationale: Two opening rest days respond appropriately to a 14-point HRV drop and poor sleep, and cycling volume returns at a reduced 20-30 minute dose rather than being replaced by an unrelated modality -- specificity is preserved even while easing load.

This is the strongest case in the family: despite excellent HRV/RHR/sleep/body-battery readings, the active pain flag and avoid_high_impact/avoid_heavy_lower_body guardrails correctly produce two opening rest days and then keep every subsequent session to guardrail-compatible cycling, bodyweight full-body, and upper-body work -- no template tagged with either active guardrail appears anywhere in the 14-day plan. A good wearable day did not override current pain, exactly as the family's calibration requires.

This plan is identical to the baseline case's, even though preferredModalityToday differs (Strength vs Cycling). As in the balanced-performance family, the same-day modality preference's effect on selection isn't observable from this comparison -- this now looks like a repeated pattern across families rather than a one-off.
suggestedChanges: Construct a comparison case where the optimizer's default choice and preferredModalityToday genuinely disagree, so the preference's real effect can be verified.

caseScores.rationale: Under a 35-minute cap, the plan contains exactly one Cycling session across the full 14 days (day 13) against six Walking sessions, despite the athlete having indoor-bike access (hasIndoorBike: true) that could support a short indoor session on far more days than walking substitutes for. For a self-described cycling-primary hybrid athlete, this is a significant specificity failure driven by time pressure, not a safety response -- nothing here is unsafe, but the plan stops looking like this athlete's plan.
suggestedChanges: Prefer a short cycling session (indoor trainer, matching the time cap) over walking when cycling is the athlete's stated primary modality and the equipment is available.

Do not let a tight time window silently displace the primary modality across the entire two-week horizon; ration the cap across cycling sessions rather than defaulting every slot to the cheapest option.

caseScores.rationale: Priority A correctly shows the strongest near-race restraint: three short race-specific sharpening sessions (20-40 min each), frequent rest days, and only one light upper-body strength session well before race week. This is exactly the near-race taper behavior an A-priority event should get.

Priority B shows less taper restraint than A (one longer race-pace session plus one taper-sharpen, versus A's three short sharpening sessions), which is the correct secondary-priority direction. Two early strength sessions are also permitted that A doesn't carry, consistent with B not needing A's full protective taper.

This is the family's clearest problem: a C-priority event, which the calibration says should not get major-peak treatment by default, instead receives TWO Race-Specific Endurance / race-pace sessions (up to 75 and 90 minutes respectively) and zero taper-sharpening sessions -- more total race-specific volume and duration than the B-priority case, and comparable to A's total race-specific time despite A using short sharpening work rather than full race-pace efforts. The A > B > C intensity/specificity gradient the family instructions describe is inverted between B and C.
suggestedChanges: Cap race-pace-category session frequency and duration more aggressively for C-priority events so total race-specific dose is clearly below B, not above it.
Reserve full race-pace sessions (as opposed to shorter taper-sharpen work) for A/B priority; a C event should look closer to normal training than to a taper.

caseScores.rationale: With the race about a month out, the plan builds genuine volume across all three disciplines (3 swim, 3 cycling including two race-specific/race-sim sessions, 2 running) plus upper- and lower-body strength, with no discipline silently substituted for another and no premature taper.

Two rest days plus mobility respond to a 14-point HRV drop, and every subsequent session is reduced-dose rather than dropped -- swimming, cycling and running all still appear across the remaining twelve days, so recovery signals scale volume without silently discarding a race discipline.

Under a 45-minute cap, all three disciplines and strength remain represented at appropriately shortened durations. One session (day 12, a 50-90 min cycling race-simulation) exceeds the stated cap; this is plausible if the cap is weekday-only and that date falls on a weekend, matching this case's own label, but I can't independently confirm the day-of-week logic from this packet alone.
suggestedChanges: If the intent is a weekday-only cap, make that explicit in the case's user-facing plan (or this packet) so it's clear the longer weekend session is intentional rather than a cap violation.

caseScores.rationale: In the final 14 days before the A-event, the plan shifts convincingly toward taper behavior: short technical-skill swim sessions, a brief cycling 'openers' session rather than a full race-simulation effort, easy running, and only one early, light upper-body strength exposure well clear of race week. All three disciplines remain present even during the taper, and nothing here reads like invented late-taper heavy load.
